strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision problem: generating music-conditioned dance videos with text control over appearance and setting, without requiring motion capture or reconstructed skeletons. Adapting an existing video generator is a practical contribution.

The architecture is coherent: zero-initialized residual audio attention preserves the base model at initialization, while LoRA enables task adaptation. The reported training cost of approximately 20 hours on one A100 suggests accessible adaptation.

Tables 1–3 report improvements over Mochi in beat alignment (8.34 to 8.89), movement realism (7.68 to 8.24), and overall consistency (8.98 to 9.39), with broadly preserved prompt adherence. The illustrated examples also support varied scene and clothing control.

The evaluation includes component ablations, explicitly held-out AIST music tracks, and 100 prompt–music combinations per configuration. The supplement provides evaluation prompts, test-track identifiers, qualitative ablations, and candid examples of anatomical failures.
weaknesses: The central synchronization claim lacks sufficiently validated evidence. All reported dance-quality scores rely on VideoLLaMA 2, without human agreement measurements, independent beat-timing metrics, or shifted/shuffled-audio controls. Audio-unconditioned Mochi already scores 8.34/10 for beat alignment, making the evaluator’s sensitivity especially important. Ground-truth videos scoring highly does not establish that the judge detects temporal synchronization. This is the principal reason the balance favors rejection.

The comparisons do not isolate learning music correspondence from ordinary dance-domain adaptation. A matched Mochi fine-tuning baseline without informative audio is absent. MM-Diffusion also generates shorter videos, and the manuscript does not sufficiently specify its training and evaluation configuration to establish a controlled comparison. Consequently, improvements in visual quality cannot be confidently attributed to the proposed conditioning design.

The ablations support trade-offs more strongly than uniformly superior components. Removing Beta-Uniform scheduling improves style alignment from 7.56 to 8.04 and beat alignment from 8.89 to 9.07, while worsening body representation. Feature addition essentially matches the full model’s beat score (8.90 versus 8.89). No uncertainty estimates accompany these scores, and zero initialization itself is not isolated from the cross-attention architecture.

Several technical rationales exceed their support. Section 4.2’s claim that homography adaptation requires increasing LoRA rank by at least eight does not follow from homography’s degrees of freedom. Appendix G selects layers using image quality under inference-time STG, but does not establish that this predicts suitability for learning audio conditioning; a comparison with randomly or uniformly selected layers at equal capacity is missing. The methodological novelty therefore rests primarily on an empirical combination of familiar mechanisms.

Important reproducibility details are missing: training resolution and frame rate, batch size, audio-token temporal alignment and positional treatment, the Beta decay rate and mapping to the backbone’s training timesteps, the actual caption-replacement probability, and sufficiently specific YouTube data provenance. The evaluator checkpoint and audiovisual sampling protocol are also unspecified, although the conclusions depend heavily on that evaluator.

Generalization claims are broader than the evidence. K-pop being absent from AIST does not establish its absence from the 15,799 YouTube training clips. Group choreography and doubled-duration generation are demonstrated qualitatively, without systematic evaluation. Likewise, seed-dependent diversity does not by itself rule out memorization. These claims should be limited to the demonstrated examples.

strengths: The task is useful: generating music-conditioned dance videos with text control directly from video training data avoids requiring motion capture or an intermediate skeleton representation.

The adaptation is technically plausible and practically accessible. Zero-initialized audio cross-attention initially preserves the pretrained network’s behavior, and training reportedly takes approximately 20 hours on one A100.

The experiments provide encouraging evidence: Table 1 reports improved beat alignment and movement realism over Mochi, while Tables 2–3 suggest largely preserved visual quality and prompt adherence. The evaluation uses held-out AIST music, and the supplement specifies the 10 tracks, 10 prompts, and evaluator questions.

The component ablations are informative. In particular, Table 3 supports including diverse training videos, and Table 4 shows that the proposed schedule improves body representation, while revealing trade-offs across metrics.
weaknesses: The central synchronization claim rests on an insufficiently validated evaluator. All principal quantitative comparisons use VideoLLaMA 2 ratings, without human agreement measurements, an independent beat-alignment measure, or shuffled/time-shifted audio controls. Audio-unconditioned Mochi already scores 8.34/10 for beat alignment, versus 8.89 for MusicInfuser and 8.95 for real videos (Table 1). This does not invalidate the improvement, but makes evaluator sensitivity critical. Ground-truth ranking alone does not establish that the metric measures temporal synchronization.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate music conditioning from dance-domain adaptation. Mochi is not matched with a dance-video fine-tuning baseline that omits audio, and MM-Diffusion differs in backbone and generated duration. Consequently, visual and movement improvements cannot be attributed cleanly to the proposed conditioning strategy. The 100-video evaluation also lacks uncertainty estimates or repeated-seed results, making small differences difficult to interpret.

The methodological justification exceeds the evidence. HR-LoRA is conventional LoRA with rank 64; the assertion that homography’s eight degrees of freedom imply an increase of at least eight in adapter rank is not established for transformer weight updates. Layer selection uses STG imaging-quality rankings without demonstrating that these predict audio adaptability or outperform equally sized random layer selections. Feature addition does not isolate the benefit of zero initialization from cross-attention itself.

Several conclusions need qualification. Removing Beta-Uniform scheduling improves style and beat alignment while worsening anatomy (Table 4), so its demonstrated benefit is a trade-off. Tempo manipulation changes pitch as well as speed, confounding the responsiveness interpretation. K-pop being absent from AIST does not establish its absence from the additional YouTube training collection, and varied outputs across seeds do not rule out memorization.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful supplementary prompts and track lists. Missing details include the default caption-replacement probability, batch size, precise noise-schedule decay and mapping, audio-video temporal encoding, and evaluator checkpoint/frame-sampling configuration. The supplied manuscript also provides no usable project-page or code URL, although it repeatedly directs readers there to assess temporal results.

Overall, the application and initial results are worthwhile, but uncertainty about whether the evaluation establishes music synchronization and whether the gains arise from the proposed adaptation outweighs the current acceptance case. These are substantive evidence gaps rather than presentation issues alone.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision problem: generating dance videos jointly controlled by music and text without requiring motion capture or reconstructed skeletons. Adapting an existing video generator is a practical contribution.

The architecture is coherent: zero-initialized audio cross-attention initially preserves the backbone’s outputs, while LoRA enables task adaptation. The reported training cost of approximately 20 hours on one A100 suggests an accessible adaptation procedure.

The reported results are encouraging. Relative to Mochi, MusicInfuser improves movement realism from 7.68 to 8.24 and overall consistency from 8.98 to 9.39, while maintaining comparable aggregate prompt alignment. These results suggest useful adaptation without wholesale loss of text control.

The experiments include component ablations, a music-disjoint AIST split, and qualitative demonstrations of tempo responsiveness, multiple dancers, diverse scenes, and longer generation. The supplement provides evaluation prompts, test-track identifiers, and candid failure examples.
weaknesses: The central synchronization claim is insufficiently validated. All principal quantitative comparisons rely on VideoLLaMA 2 scores, without human agreement measurements, objective motion–beat alignment, or tests showing sensitivity to shifted or mismatched audio. Mochi, which cannot hear the music, already scores 8.34 for beat alignment versus 8.89 for MusicInfuser. Real videos receiving high scores is only a plausibility check; it does not establish that the evaluator measures precise synchronization.

The experiments do not adequately separate music conditioning from dance-domain fine-tuning. A matched adaptation baseline trained without audio, or inference with shuffled/removed audio, is absent. Consequently, improvements over the unadapted Mochi model could partly reflect additional dance training. The qualitative tempo experiment changes pitch as well as speed and does not quantify temporal alignment.

Evidence for the individual technical contributions is mixed. In Table 4, removing Beta-Uniform scheduling improves both style and beat alignment, although anatomy worsens; feature addition also slightly exceeds the full model on both alignment scores. These results support quality trade-offs more clearly than superior audio alignment. The homography-degree-of-freedom argument does not establish a required LoRA weight-update rank, and selecting layers using imaging quality is not directly validated as an audio-adaptability criterion.

Evaluation uncertainty limits interpretation of the modest gains. The benchmark contains 100 videos formed from only ten music tracks and ten prompts, with no confidence intervals or repeated-run analysis. Group choreography and longer generation are demonstrated qualitatively rather than systematically assessed. Calling K-pop unseen is also insufficiently justified because the styles present in the 15,799 YouTube training clips are not documented.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful supplementary material: the manuscript omits the default caption-replacement probability, batch size, training resolution/frame rate, exact Beta decay schedule, detailed audio projector configuration, and sufficient identification of the YouTube data. Overall, the practical idea and promising examples are worthwhile, but uncertainty about whether the method achieves its core synchronization objective currently outweighs the acceptance case.

strengths: The task is useful and relevant: generating music-conditioned dance videos directly, without motion capture or intermediate skeletons, while retaining text control over appearance and setting. Adapting an existing video model is a practical contribution.

The framework is coherent and computationally accessible. It combines selectively placed audio cross-attention, LoRA, and a noise-sampling curriculum, with reported training of 4,000 steps in approximately 20 hours on one A100.

The ablations cover several meaningful alternatives, including first/middle/last/evenly distributed/all-layer adaptation, feature addition, initialization, scheduling, and training-data composition. The selected layers achieve the highest overall scores under both automated evaluators (Tables 1 and 5).

There is encouraging empirical evidence: Table 2 reports improved beat alignment and movement realism over the Mochi backbone, while the 33-participant study reports 82.1% preference over MM-Diffusion for music–dance alignment. The manuscript also provides evaluation prompts, held-out music identifiers, and explicit failure cases.
weaknesses: The central synchronization claim depends heavily on insufficiently validated Video-LLM ratings. Figure 9 demonstrates aggregate human preference against one baseline, but does not report the claimed correlation between automated scores and human judgments. There are no shifted/shuffled-audio controls establishing sensitivity to temporal alignment. Qwen3-Omni also assigns the full model 10.00 for body representation and 9.96 for consistency, raising concerns about score saturation. These weaknesses materially limit interpretation of the main quantitative results.

The comparisons do not cleanly separate learning music correspondence from improving dance generation through additional training. Mochi lacks audio conditioning, while MM-Diffusion differs substantially in backbone and output characteristics. An otherwise matched adaptation trained or evaluated with absent, shuffled, or mismatched audio would provide a much stronger causal test. Human evaluation does not compare against Mochi or the principal adapter ablations.

The proposed layer-adaptability criterion has a plausible motivation but an unestablished mechanism. Supplement G selects layers using image quality under inference-time skip guidance; this is not directly a measure of their suitability for learning audio-conditioned motion. The positional baselines provide useful empirical support, but there is no analysis relating the score to adaptation benefit across layers or random subsets. Claims of a principled adaptability measure and preservation of the denoising manifold exceed the evidence.

The reliability of relatively small ablation gains is unclear. Evaluation uses 100 videos formed from only 10 music tracks and 10 prompts, without confidence intervals or repeated-training results. Some component effects vary by evaluator: removing Beta-Uniform scheduling improves VideoLLaMA 2 style and beat alignment in Table 6, although it reduces body representation. The evidence supports a quality trade-off more clearly than uniformly improved musical alignment.

Important reproducibility and efficiency details are missing, including training resolution/frame rate, batch size, LoRA target modules, the precise beta-decay schedule, the default caption-replacement probability, and access details for the YouTube collection. Layer-scoring prompts, guidance settings, and precomputation cost are also insufficiently specified. Reporting total training time alone does not substantiate the claimed computational savings relative to other adaptation strategies.

Overall, the practical system and breadth of ablations are worthwhile. However, the unresolved validity of the synchronization evaluation and the limited isolation of the proposed mechanism currently outweigh those merits. This recommendation is driven by uncertainty about the central claims, rather than by a requirement to exceed a benchmark or evaluate many more datasets.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: generating dance videos conditioned jointly on music and text without requiring intermediate skeletal motion. Adapting a pretrained video model offers practical advantages for controlling appearance, environment, and subjects.

The adaptation design is coherent. Sparse zero-initialized cross-attention, LoRA, and the proposed noise curriculum provide a plausible approach to adding audio conditioning while retaining pretrained capabilities. The reported training cost of approximately 20 hours on one A100 is attractive.

The experiments include meaningful component ablations and several layer-placement baselines. The proposed layer selection achieves the highest aggregate score under both Qwen3-Omni and VideoLLaMA 2, providing empirical support beyond a single evaluator.

Results indicate useful improvements: Table 2 reports beat alignment of 8.89 versus Mochi's 8.34, and movement realism of 8.24 versus 7.68. The 33-participant study also strongly favors MusicInfuser over MM-Diffusion. Held-out music tracks, disclosed evaluation prompts, and qualitative examples of varied subjects and settings are additional positives.
weaknesses: The central synchronization claim is insufficiently validated. Most quantitative evidence consists of Video-LLM ratings without tests showing sensitivity to temporal alignment, such as shifting or replacing the soundtrack for the same video. Mochi, which receives no audio, already scores 8.34 for beat alignment compared with 8.95 for ground truth, making metric calibration particularly important. Figure 7 provides qualitative tempo-response evidence, but changing playback speed also changes pitch, and no quantitative movement-tempo analysis separates these effects.

The claimed correlation between automated metrics and human judgments is not demonstrated. Figure 9 reports aggregate preferences against MM-Diffusion, rather than correlations on individual examples or rankings across configurations. There is no human comparison against Mochi or the adapter ablations, so the study does not validate the relatively small automated differences supporting the main methodological claims. Evaluator disagreement also warrants investigation: the full model receives body-representation scores of 10.00 from Qwen3-Omni and 7.16 from VideoLLaMA 2.

The layer-adaptability criterion has a promising empirical result but a weakly established interpretation. Section G selects layers using imaging quality under inference-time skip guidance; this does not itself establish that those layers are best suited to learning music-motion correspondence or preserving the pretrained distribution. Tables 1 and 5 compare sensible placements, but omit random subsets, repeated training runs, and uncertainty estimates. The VideoLLaMA 2 aggregate advantage over middle-layer placement is only 8.33 versus 8.21. Thus, the evidence supports a useful heuristic more clearly than the claimed principled characterization of adaptability.

Baseline comparisons do not fully isolate the source of improvement. MM-Diffusion differs substantially in pretrained capability and generated duration, while unadapted Mochi cannot use audio. The same-backbone ablations help, but a dance-finetuned, text-only LoRA control is missing; consequently, improved motion realism and consistency cannot be cleanly attributed to music conditioning rather than dance-domain adaptation. The human study against MM-Diffusion alone leaves this ambiguity unresolved.

Several implementation details necessary for reproduction are missing, including the exact selected layer indices, LoRA target modules, training resolution/frame rate and batch size, the Beta-schedule decay specification, and the default caption-replacement probability. The YouTube playlists and clip-selection procedure are also insufficiently specified. Claims of generalization to unseen music categories are primarily qualitative, and the presence of those categories in the additional YouTube training data is not established.

A minor reporting error is that Figure 9's choreography preferences sum to 102%. More consequentially, the current recommendation is driven by insufficient validation of synchronization and of the evaluation framework underpinning the technical claims. These concerns outweigh the worthwhile adaptation contribution, yielding a weak reject rather than a rejection based merely on limited benchmark breadth.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision problem: generating dance videos conditioned on both music and text without requiring motion capture or an intermediate skeleton representation. Adapting Mochi preserves access to its visual and motion priors while enabling flexible scene and appearance control.

The proposed layer-selection heuristic is computationally appealing. Selecting 16 of 48 layers using skip-guidance imaging quality avoids combinatorial training searches. Table 1 supports its practical value: the selected configuration achieves an overall score of 8.14 versus 7.62 for evenly distributed adapters and 7.80 for adapting all layers.

The experiments include substantial component analysis: adapter placement, feature addition, zero initialization, noise scheduling, LoRA capacity, and in-the-wild data. A second evaluator in Tables 5–6 provides additional support for the overall configuration, although individual metric trends vary.

The reported training cost—approximately 20 hours on one A100—is attractive. Evaluation uses held-out AIST music, and the qualitative examples illustrate potentially useful capabilities including multiple dancers, unusual subjects, tempo responsiveness, and generation up to nine seconds.
The 33-participant human study provides evidence of improvement over MM-Diffusion, with reported preferences of 82.1% for music–dance alignment and 85.8% for motion realism.
weaknesses: The central synchronization claim depends heavily on insufficiently validated video-LLM ratings. Figure 9 reports aggregate preferences against MM-Diffusion, rather than an actual correlation between automated scores and human judgments. There are no shifted-audio or mismatched-audio controls demonstrating sensitivity to temporal alignment. Mochi, which receives no audio, already scores 8.34 for beat alignment versus 8.89 for the proposed method, making evaluator calibration particularly important.

The human comparison does not isolate the benefit of the proposed adaptation strategy: MM-Diffusion differs substantially in backbone, visual quality, and output duration. Human comparisons against Mochi and simpler adapters on the same backbone are absent. Consequently, the strongest human evidence establishes an advantage over that baseline but does not validate the main methodological choices.

The interpretation of skip-guidance imaging quality as layer 'adaptability' remains heuristic. Section G selects layers using VBench imaging quality, but does not establish that this quantity predicts successful audio–motion adaptation. The placement ablations support the selected configuration; they do not establish the broader claims about preserving the denoising manifold or identifying motion-relevant layers. Zero-initialized cross-attention and LoRA are established components, so the evidential support for this selection principle matters to the originality claim.

The evaluation contains only ten distinct test music tracks, paired with ten prompts, and provides no uncertainty estimates or repeated-training results. Several gains are small, and some are evaluator-dependent: without Beta-Uniform scheduling, VideoLLaMA 2 reports better style and beat alignment, although worse body representation. Claims of significant superiority and generalization to unseen music categories are stronger than the quantitative evidence supports.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful prompt and music-code listings. The manuscript omits training resolution/frame rate, batch size, the exact scheduling decay, default caption-replacement probability, detailed layer-scoring settings, and identifiers for the four YouTube playlists. It also does not quantify layer-scoring overhead or provide comparative memory and training-cost measurements.

Overall, the practical contribution and component experiments are worthwhile, but uncertainty in the measurement of music synchronization and limited validation of the central layer-selection principle keep the recommendation at the decision boundary.
